title: The living homelab
subtitle: An evolving personal infrastructure ecosystem
summary: Routing, Linux, storage, containers and home automation—brought together on repurposed hardware, one useful system at a time.
nextIteration: Document the service inventory and recovery procedure; expand network observability; measure the camera playback path before changing it.

sections.heading: Why build a lab?
sections.body: The lab makes infrastructure tangible. A network, a storage system and a collection of services became a place to test how software behaves on physical hardware. It is personal infrastructure with ongoing maintenance, rather than a production availability claim.

sections.heading: Separate the responsibilities
sections.body: A dedicated pfSense router handles network control. The main Linux server hosts Docker Compose services. Three separate laptop motherboards form the Kubernetes lab, so cluster experiments do not require moving every household service onto Kubernetes.

sections.heading: A service ecosystem
sections.body: Jellyfin and Immich handle media and photos. Frigate and go2rtc support camera recording and streaming experiments. Home Assistant connects the smart-home layer. Portainer, Homepage, Snipe-IT, Netdata, Nginx Proxy Manager and Authelia support administration, visibility and application access.

sections.heading: Storage changes over time
sections.body: The storage design has changed across generations. Earlier records describe mirrored SSDs; later notes describe a different boot-storage arrangement. This archive deliberately avoids presenting either historical layout as a verified current topology. Redundancy, backup and restore testing remain separate concerns.

sections.heading: Smaller builds inside the system
sections.body: MagicMirror is documented as a running container. Display quality and ambient brightness are separate hardware investigations. Self-hosted Overleaf work includes a created first user and a completed TeX installation in the September record. These are service milestones within the lab, rather than separate flagship projects.

sections.heading: Still being investigated
sections.body: Recent camera work concerns main-stream recording, sub-stream detection and playback on different clients. Maintaining recording quality while controlling transcoding load is an active design question. Proposed inventory generation, local AI summaries, WAN/LAN monitoring and doorbell integrations remain future iterations.

updates.title: Service ecosystem recorded
updates.body: Container output documented the camera, automation, media, display and monitoring stacks. A running container is not treated as an uptime guarantee.

title: Three boards. One cluster.
subtitle: Kubernetes on repurposed laptop motherboards
summary: Three repurposed laptop motherboards, roughly 48 GB of RAM, and a documented load test with 290 running pods.
nextIteration: Make thermal and resource measurements repeatable, and resolve the recorded Metrics API gap before drawing conclusions about headroom.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body: Build a physical cluster from hardware already available: three laptop motherboards from different CPU generations, integrated into a custom shared enclosure. Approximately 16 GB of RAM per node gives the lab roughly 48 GB in total.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.body: Three Linux nodes connect over Ethernet to form a Kubernetes environment. A virtual API endpoint provides cluster access. Public diagrams use K8S-01, K8S-02 and K8S-03 rather than publishing internal addresses.

sections.heading: Historical software snapshot
sections.body: The July–August 2026 record names Kubernetes v1.34.9 and containerd 2.2.2. These are historical software details, not a live inventory.

sections.heading: The workload experiment
sections.body: A kube-burner v2.8.1 run reached 290 running pods, distributed 99, 93 and 98 across the three nodes. The visualization reproduces those counts. It does not claim a maximum cluster capacity, production benchmark or sustained performance guarantee.

sections.heading: Physical constraints
sections.body: The boards share a compact enclosure and fan. Different CPU generations and a 100 Mbps switch make thermal behaviour and network capacity meaningful constraints to investigate.

sections.heading: Open investigation
sections.body: The metrics API was unavailable during a documented kubectl top check. Thermal monitoring and the metrics pipeline remain areas to validate before drawing conclusions about resource headroom.

updates.title: A physical three-node cluster
updates.body: User-confirmed cluster work included three control-plane/etcd nodes, kube-vip and Cilium.

updates.title: 290 pods in a recorded test
updates.body: The July–August snapshot records a kube-burner test with 99, 93 and 98 pods across three nodes. This is one test result, not a capacity guarantee.

nextIteration: Measure CPU use and playback behavior on the intended screen before increasing frame rate or tile quality.

sections.heading: Start with the client constraint
sections.body: An older Android TV box cannot be assumed to support a modern video frontend. The public implementation uses conservative HTML, CSS and JavaScript and a 1280 × 720-oriented dashboard.

sections.heading: Convert once, share the frames
sections.body: The server opens a read-only camera sub-stream and runs one FFmpeg worker per configured camera. Browser clients share that worker’s output rather than starting an independent transcode for every viewer.

sections.heading: Keep recording independent
sections.body: The camera dashboard is a compatibility display path. Frigate recording remains independent. The architecture separates the high-quality recording path from the lower-bandwidth MJPEG copy used by the kiosk.

sections.heading: Beyond camera tiles
sections.body: The implementation supports optional solar telemetry, cached weather and a local clock. These are separate signals, allowing a missing optional data source to be represented independently.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs
sections.body: MJPEG supports older clients, but conversion consumes server resources and repeated JPEG frames use bandwidth. The documented resolution and frame-rate controls are tuning options, not a promise of measured performance.

updates.title: Compatibility dashboard implemented
updates.body: Public source documents shared FFmpeg workers, MJPEG tiles and optional telemetry.

title: Making the lab observable
subtitle: Metrics, dashboards and the next network layer
summary: Prometheus and Grafana make host and service behavior visible. Log health and WAN/LAN availability are the next parts to strengthen.
nextIteration: Add and validate network exporters, investigate log-stack health and record what each availability probe can actually distinguish.

sections.heading: From inspection to observation
sections.body: Netdata is part of the lab. By July 2026, the user had confirmed a Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Node Exporter setup; later September notes confirm Prometheus and Grafana were already configured. The older portfolio label of “planned” was therefore stale.

sections.heading: Different signals, different roles
sections.body: Prometheus collects metrics and Grafana presents them. Loki is the log component, but later container output recorded restart behavior. Presence in a Compose stack is not evidence of uninterrupted service or complete log coverage.

sections.heading: The next boundary
sections.body: pfSense SNMP and Blackbox probes were proposed to distinguish WAN reachability from LAN availability. Those exporters and the resulting downtime views are planned work, not confirmed deployed monitoring.

sections.heading: What to learn next
sections.body: Measurements should answer a concrete question: whether a failure is at the host, service or network layer. Each added dashboard needs a known signal source and a test that the failure is actually visible.

updates.title: Network monitoring remains next

title: From inbox to report
subtitle: Self-hosted reporting with a portable output
summary: Mail ingestion, browser rendering and structured data become a repeatable CSV reporting workflow.

sections.heading: The recurring task
sections.body: Collect inputs, extract useful fields and produce a repeatable report. The public record describes the integration pattern; source messages, recipients and organization-specific logic stay private.

sections.heading: The working path
sections.body: A self-hosted n8n workflow ingests email over IMAP. Local Express services and Playwright/Chromium handle content that requires browser rendering. Extracted records become a CSV deliverable.

sections.heading: A constraint changed the design
sections.body: A planned spreadsheet API integration was unavailable. CSV delivery provided a working route without requiring that integration. Separating extraction from output made this substitution possible.

sections.heading: What the result establishes
sections.body: The recorded workflow established the CSV reporting path. The archive does not assign unsupported time savings, throughput, business impact or adoption numbers.

updates.title: CSV reporting route established
updates.body: Mail ingestion, browser rendering and structured extraction were connected to portable report output.

nextIteration: Continue device testing, review data boundaries and complete the documented release prerequisites.

sections.heading: Write first
sections.body: The current repository describes a native Android client for Samsung devices with S Pen support. Handwritten input, pressure-aware ink, undo/redo and local history form the core interaction.

sections.heading: Keep the inference choice explicit
sections.body: Writing-only mode does not need an AI provider. Optional modes include an on-device model, a local server, a private proxy and a compatible remote API. These paths have different data boundaries.

sections.heading: An evolving fork
sections.body: The project originated as a fork of MaximeRivest/riddle. The original reMarkable implementation is preserved while this fork develops the Android diary. The upstream lineage is credited rather than treated as wholly original software.

sections.heading: Current scope
sections.body: The repository is under active development. A public store release is not established; the README lists signing, device testing, privacy material and a review of naming/artwork rights as release work. iOS is a plan, not an implemented platform.

updates.title: Android is the active implementation
updates.body: Current source describes the S Pen client and optional AI paths, with reMarkable preserved for reference.

title: Smart Hat
subtitle: Smart Hat
summary: An embedded vision concept connecting camera input to processing and speech for a person with visual impairment.

sections.heading: Intent
sections.body: Smart Hat explored how camera and sensor input could become audio information about a person's surroundings. It connects embedded hardware, image-processing ideas and mobile integration.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.body: An ESP32-CAM and microcontroller/sensor components provide input. Processing concepts convert visual information into data that can be delivered as speech.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: This is a historical experimental concept. Clinical effectiveness, safety as a navigation aid, completed commercial-product status and real-world deployment are not established by the available record.

sections.heading: Engineering connection
sections.body: The same camera → processing → useful output relationship reappears in later local-vision and home-automation experiments.

title: Messages across trust boundaries
subtitle: Decentralized encrypted chat · Final-year project
summary: A university project exploring encrypted communication and decentralized data handling through blockchain concepts.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The final-year project at MUET brought application development, cryptography and blockchain concepts into a decentralized encrypted chat application.

sections.heading: Design
sections.body: The project explored encrypted message data and blockchain-backed tamper resistance. Solidity, Python, web technologies, React Native and database components formed the historical technology set.

sections.heading: Trust boundaries
sections.body: Encryption, key handling and distributed state solve different problems. The illustration distinguishes message encryption from propagation through a distributed network; it is a conceptual view, not a new security specification.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: AES-256 and decentralized data handling were part of the project exploration. No independent security audit, production deployment or claim of invulnerability is made.

title: The network foundation
subtitle: Home distribution & access network
summary: pfSense, x64 hardware and multiple interfaces formed an earlier generation of the home network.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.body: A distribution/access-layer network used pfSense on x64 hardware with multiple interfaces. Areas included cameras, media, personal systems and wireless connectivity.

sections.heading: Engineering focus
sections.body: Routing, firewall and DNS configuration established boundaries between different uses of the same physical network.

sections.heading: Evolution
sections.body: This project belongs to the lineage of the current homelab. The lab explorer's evolution control follows that growth from a network foundation to containers, Kubernetes and automation.

title: A home for the data
subtitle: Home NAS & media server
summary: An earlier TrueNAS environment combined network storage, media and home-automation experiments.

sections.heading: First generation
sections.body: An x64 machine and multiple drives became a NAS and media environment. RAID storage, network file access and media streaming shared a home with Home Assistant and Frigate-related experiments.

sections.heading: Iteration
sections.body: The modern Linux and Docker-based home server is a later generation of that idea. The common thread is connecting storage to services while learning the operational tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Storage lesson
sections.body: Redundancy, backup and recovery are separate concerns. This archive records the platform evolution without asserting an unverified backup or recovery guarantee.

title: At the hardware boundary
subtitle: USB & Wi-Fi Ducky experiments
summary: Microcontrollers, custom circuit work and HID behaviour explored through a controlled security experiment.

sections.heading: The experiment
sections.body: This project combined open-source concepts with microcontroller and circuit work to explore how USB HID and Wi-Fi-controlled embedded functionality behave.

sections.heading: Engineering focus
sections.body: The interesting boundary is between firmware, an interface trusted by the operating system and physical hardware. Public documentation remains at the architecture and learning level.

sections.heading: Source lineage
sections.body: The public Wi-Fi Ducky repository is a fork of an existing open-source project. It is credited as source lineage rather than presented as entirely original software.

title: Code reaches the room
subtitle: DIY smart home
summary: A network-connected microcontroller experiment for room lighting and fan control.

sections.heading: Intent
sections.body: Control room lighting and a fan through network connectivity and a microcontroller. The project explored integration with Google Home and Google Assistant concepts.

sections.heading: The signal path
sections.body: A command crosses the network, reaches the controller and changes a physical output. The diagram makes that software-to-hardware boundary visible.

sections.heading: Connection to the present
sections.body: Later Home Assistant work grows from the same curiosity about connecting services to physical devices. This record does not assert current interoperability for the historical prototype.
